claims.text: Special quasi-random structures can be used to model defect-free bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
DFT including spin-orbit coupling can provide accurate electronic states for HfNbTaTiZr transport calculations.
A linearized Boltzmann transport equation can calculate the electronic transport properties.
Green–Kubo calculations using on-the-fly machine-learned force fields can calculate lattice thermal conductivity.
Combining DFT, Boltzmann electronic transport, and Green–Kubo lattice transport will independently quantify the electronic and lattice contributions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Below 200 K, the electronic and lattice thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Special quasi-random structures accurately represent intrinsic atomic-scale disorder and force-constant fluctuations in HfNbTaTiZr.
Machine-learned-force-field molecular dynamics can capture phonon dynamics at arbitrary order.
The Green–Kubo method with machine-learned force fields accounts for complex phonon scattering, including force-constant fluctuations.
The Boltzmann transport calculation isolates the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution.
The predicted lattice thermal conductivity will be lower than prior conflated estimates.
The predicted lattice thermal conductivity will have weak temperature dependence.
The lattice thermal conductivity will be below approximately 1 W/(K·m) at mid-to-high temperatures.
Electronic thermal conductivity will dominate below 200 K.
The new method will reduce total thermal-conductivity prediction error by about 20–30% relative to previous models.
Existing analytical models conflate lattice and electronic heat transport, often through use of the Wiedemann–Franz law without detailed atomistic phonon scattering.
Existing models have especially large discrepancies with experiment in the low-temperature regime.
The model is applicable from 200 to 1200 K to defect-free or well-characterized oxygen-containing bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
Additional impurities, significant defects, nanoscale dimensions, structural deviations, or temperatures outside 200–1200 K may cause prediction deviations.
Force-field training and temperature extrapolation introduce an uncertainty of approximately ±20%.

contradictions.description: The conditions specify simulations extending below 200 K, whereas the boundary states that the model is outside its validity range below 200 K.
The conditions describe lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K as comparable, while the predicted outcome says the electronic contribution dominates below 200 K.
